name: CTCMath
line: CTCMath teaches by video, then asks the lesson's questions; AMP places each learner and chooses every next problem.
description: AMP vs CTCMath: price, placement, review and evidence. CTCMath teaches K-12 by short video; AMP finds the level and chooses every next problem.
verdict: CTCMath is a low-priced K-12 video course with more than 1,400 short tutorials, and it reaches calculus [1][3]. Lessons follow the course or the adult's assignments, most questions are multiple choice, and grades 1 to 8 add a weekly review set [2][5][14]. AMP places each learner, chooses every problem from the learner's answers, checks typed answers exactly and brings each old skill back on its own schedule.

reasons.title: AMP finds the level, so the adult doesn't have to
reasons.body: CTCMath's placement tests cover one topic at a time in K-8 and return a list of lessons that may need review [2]. Cathy Duffy notes that the program does not automatically prescribe a grade level or course from the tests [4]. The adult can then assign lessons with due dates [5][9]. AMP places the learner within the first 24 problems and keeps a level in each of 14 strands of math, with no separate test, and keeps adjusting at every answer.

reasons.title: Practice first, and help at the problem
reasons.body: Each CTCMath lesson opens with a video tutorial of about 4 to 9 minutes, and the questions follow [1][4]. A student with a low score can rewatch the tutorial and try a new set [4][5]. AMP starts with the problem. Help comes at the point of need: a one-step hint that never gives the answer, a written lesson with a worked example, and a narrated film for a growing share of problem types.

reasons.title: Typed answers, checked exactly
reasons.body: Most CTCMath worksheets use multiple choice [2]. A review site notes that CTCMath adds extra wrong answers to discourage guessing, and that students can sometimes work backward from the choices [5]. Some Algebra and Geometry lessons are self-graded against worked solutions [2][5]. In AMP, 547 of 1,384 problem types need a typed number, a fraction, lines of work, a plotted point or a built model. Every answer is checked exactly, and AMP's level estimate allows for the chance of a lucky guess on a choice question.

reasons.title: Review timed to each learner's own answers
reasons.body: CTCMath's lesson list gives grades 1 to 8 each 32 Weekly Revision Tasks [5][14], and Cathy Duffy describes printable weekly review sheets of 26 problems [4]. We found none in its Kindergarten or high school courses [14]. More review is a set the adult builds in the Question Bank Wizard, by topic, difficulty and length [4]. We found nothing in its published materials that times review to a learner's own answers [1][2][14]. AMP brings each learned skill back after 6 hours, 1 day, 3 days, 1 week, 2 weeks and a month, mixed with other topics. A miss restarts that skill's schedule.

reasons.title: One bar for learned, and help doesn't count
reasons.body: In CTCMath the parent sets the passing score and how many attempts come before worked solutions appear [9]. Its Mastery feature rewards students who try more questions at higher difficulty [2]. In AMP a skill is Strong when four of the last five answers are right without help. An answer given after a hint or the lesson does not count. Two misses in a row send practice back to what the skill builds on, and anyone can read the rule in AMP's public source code.

reasons.title: Workbooks made from the learner's own record
reasons.body: CTCMath's Question Bank Wizard prints worksheets by the topic, difficulty and length the adult chooses [4]. AMP composes each workbook from the learner's own answers: a warm-up, a short lesson, practice, the skills due for review and a challenge. Each comes with a worked answer key, and results entered from paper count toward the learner's level.

rows.price: One student: $257 a year or $39.90 a month. Family: $397 a year or $59.90 a month. Full refund within 365 days [6].
rows.buyers: Families and teachers, with a free trial [7]. Says it is an approved vendor for multiple state ESA/EFA programs and charter schools; the pages we read name none [1][8].
rows.range: Kindergarten through calculus, every grade in one membership [2][3].
rows.start: Optional placement tests by topic in K-8 list lessons to review. They do not automatically prescribe a grade or course [2][4].
rows.teaching: A video tutorial of 4 to 9 minutes from one teacher, then questions, with worked solutions after submitting [1][4].
rows.next: The course order, or lessons the adult assigns with due dates [5][9]. Reviewers say questions get easier or harder with performance [4][5].
rows.mastery: A passing score the parent sets, and how many attempts come before solutions appear [9]. A Mastery feature rewards more questions at higher difficulty [2].
rows.review: 32 Weekly Revision Tasks a grade in grades 1 to 8, weekly review sheets of 26 problems, and question sets the adult builds [4][5][14]. None timed to a learner's answers found [1][2].
rows.print: One-page lesson summaries, worked solutions, review sheets, and worksheets built by topic, difficulty and length [1][4].
rows.adult: Can assign lessons and due dates, set passing scores and attempts, and print worksheets [4][5][9]. Some Algebra and Geometry lessons are self-graded [2].
rows.reports: Every lesson attempt with pass or fail, score and time [1]. A weekly emailed report and printable certificates [2][4].
rows.evidence: No outcome study found on the pages we read. No entry in Evidence for ESSA or the What Works Clearinghouse as of November 2026 [10][11].

theirs: CTCMath is an online math course for kindergarten through grade 12. Cathy Duffy's review says Australian math teacher Patrick Murray created it and teaches it [4]. The company lists more than 1,400 tutorials and says more than 217,000 students have joined [1]. One membership opens every course: K-8, Algebra 1, Geometry, Algebra II, Pre-Calculus with Trigonometry, and Calculus [2][3].

A lesson starts with a tutorial of about 4 to 9 minutes, narrated over synchronized animation [1]. Then the learner answers interactive questions, marked automatically with worked solutions after submitting, or works an optional printable worksheet [1]. A one-page summary prints with each tutorial, and a speaker icon reads questions aloud [1][4]. Grades 1 to 8 each include 32 Weekly Revision Tasks [5][14]. Reward ribbons in bronze, silver, gold and platinum mark the level of accomplishment [4].

Parents can assign lessons with due dates, set the passing score, and set how many attempts come before solutions appear [5][9]. Placement tests for each K-8 topic list lessons that may need review [2]. Progress reports show each attempt, pass or fail, score and time spent, and a weekly report can go out by email [1][2].
credit: A lower price. The family membership is $397 a year for several students, every grade through calculus, with a full refund within 365 days [2][6]. AMP is $599 a year for the first child and refunds within 30 days.
Far more video. More than 1,400 short tutorials from one teacher [1][4]. AMP has narrated films for a growing share of its problem types, not a video for every lesson.
Questions read aloud with a speaker icon [4]. AMP has no read-aloud.
Parent controls: due dates, passing scores, and attempts before solutions appear [5][9].

theirs: We found no outcome study of CTCMath on the pages of its site we read or in a search for studies of it: no randomized trial, no comparison-group study, no usage study. CTCMath has no entry in Evidence for ESSA or the What Works Clearinghouse as of November 2026 [10][11].

Its homeschool page lists its benefits as what parents report, with no data [3]. The homepage says families can "start seeing results as early as the very first lesson" [7]. The page cites no data for it.
ours: AMP's review rule comes from a trial that holds up. In a randomized trial of 787 seventh graders, mixed, spaced practice scored 62% on a test a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks; the What Works Clearinghouse says it meets its standards without reservations, though the test was the researchers' own [12]. On watching versus doing, the best data are weaker: in an online psychology course for adults, students who did more interactive activities learned more than students who watched more video or read more pages. The authors estimate the benefit of extra doing at more than six times that of extra watching or reading; the data are correlational [13]. We think a program that starts with the problem and times review to each skill will do better than one that starts with a video and reviews by the week. That is our bet, and we have committed to testing it in public.

AMP is new, and its own outcome studies have not run yet. They begin in 2027: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. Until then, the research behind each part of AMP is laid out in our report, and the code is public.

them: You want one low price for several children, all the way to calculus.
Your child likes to watch a teacher explain a topic before trying it.
Your child needs questions read aloud.
Your education-fund program approves CTCMath and not AMP.
amp: You want the program, not you, to place your child and choose each problem.
You want typed answers checked exactly, and help that never counts as mastery.
You want each old skill to come back on its own schedule, timed to your child's answers.
Your child is ahead in one part of math and behind in another.
You want printed workbooks built from your child's own practice, with worked answer keys.

questions.question: Is CTCMath cheaper than AMP?
questions.answer: Yes. CTCMath is $257 a year for one student or $397 a year for a family [6]. AMP is $599 a year for the first child and $399 for each more, and the account holder and a second parent practice free. The price buys a program that finds the level, chooses every problem, schedules review and prints unlimited workbooks from counting to precalculus.

questions.question: Does CTCMath adapt to my child?
questions.answer: Reviewers say questions get easier or harder with a student's performance [4][5]. Cathy Duffy notes that its tests do not automatically prescribe a grade level or course, and the adult can assign lessons [4][5]. AMP keeps a level in each of 14 strands and chooses every next problem from the learner's answers.

questions.question: Is there research showing CTCMath works?
questions.answer: We found no outcome study on the pages of its site we read, and it has no entry in Evidence for ESSA or the What Works Clearinghouse as of November 2026 [10][11]. AMP's rationale and the research behind each part are in our report.

questions.question: Does AMP teach calculus?
questions.answer: No. AMP runs from counting through precalculus. CTCMath's membership includes Calculus [3].

questions.question: Can my child watch CTCMath videos and practice in AMP?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places the learner within the first 24 problems and keeps a level in each strand, whatever else a learner uses.
